title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Monroe Twp fights a $300M suit over its data center ban—what it means for power, water and towns nearby.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're looking at Monroe Township's push in federal court to end a $300 million lawsuit from a data center developer after the township banned new facilities.
That sounds like a big one. Why is this case drawing attention from people 30 miles away in southeast Michigan?
Because the outcome could decide whether other local governments can keep these projects out when they pull huge amounts of power and water.
Walk me through what happened. The township banned new data centers, the developer sued for $300 million, and now Monroe wants the judge to toss the whole thing?
Exactly. The developer claims the ban blocks a project that was already in the works. Monroe says local zoning rules give them the right to decide what lands in their community.
How did we get here? When did these projects start showing up in Michigan townships?

Over the last few years, companies have been scouting rural spots for the massive facilities needed to run AI and cloud computing. They need steady power in the hundreds of megawatts and lots of water for cooling.
What does that kind of demand do to the local grid and residents' bills?

One large data center can use as much electricity as a small city. Utilities sometimes have to upgrade lines or build new generation, and those costs can show up in monthly bills for everyone in the region.
And water? I've heard cooling towers use millions of gallons.
Yes, and in areas already watching drought or aquifer levels, that raises real concerns for farmers and homeowners who rely on the same sources.
What about farmland? These projects often want flat open land that used to grow crops.
Right. Once rezoned industrial, that ground is usually lost for agriculture. Nearby towns worry about noise, traffic, and property values shifting too.
So Monroe's ban is trying to protect all of that. Why is the developer fighting so hard with a $300 million claim?
They argue the township changed the rules after investments were made, and they want compensation or the project allowed. The case is testing how much say locals really have.
If the judge sides with the township and dismisses the suit, what happens next for other communities watching this?
It could give other townships more confidence to pass similar bans or moratoriums without fearing big lawsuits. If the developer wins, it might chill local efforts to push back.
We've seen several other places reject projects this week. Is this lawsuit connected to that wave of opposition?
Not directly, but the same worries about power, water, and land are showing up everywhere. Monroe's case could become a template or a warning.
Any sense of timeline? When might we hear a ruling?
Federal cases like this can take months. Both sides are filing motions now, so the next few weeks will show how strong each argument looks.
For listeners 30 miles away, why should they pay attention even if they're not in Monroe?
Because the grid is regional. A big new load in one township can affect reliability and rates across southeast Michigan, and a precedent here travels fast.
Got it. Let's shift to some of the other results that came in today and yesterday.
A candidate who ran against data center growth beat the incumbent in a Democratic primary for state House. That win moves the debate into Lansing for that district.
Voters clearly sent a signal there. How might that change things at the state level?
The new representative can push bills on power demand, tax incentives, or local control. It gives opponents a stronger voice in committee hearings.
Washtenaw voters also turned down a billion-dollar rezoning in a rural township near Ann Arbor.
Yes, residents blocked the project over concerns about farmland loss and heavy infrastructure strain. The vote keeps the land agricultural for now.
And in the congressional race, Will Lawrence defeated Haley Stevens in the MI-7 primary after campaigning hard against large data centers.
That result sends the issue to Washington. The new representative can raise questions about federal tax breaks and grid impacts that cross state lines.
Holland-area voters rejected a project at the ballot box too, ending months of debate over noise and power use.
The defeat shows that even after site plans advance, organized local opposition can still stop things. Nearby townships are watching that precedent closely.
In Mason, voters narrowed the city council field in a race where the data center fight was front and center.
Eight candidates remain. The November winners will decide whether the proposed project in Ingham County moves ahead or stays on hold.
Another primary win went to a moratorium supporter, pushing the statewide fight into Congress as well.
Voters in districts facing new proposals now have someone who made blocking unchecked growth a campaign promise.
Yesterday, Augusta Township voters overturned a rezoning that would have put a data center on farmland.
That keeps the property agricultural and avoids the noise, power, and water demands that would have come with it.
Independence Township approved a moratorium stopping new proposals while they write rules.
The pause gives Oakland County residents time to figure out acceptable limits on power, water, and land use. Other towns may copy the approach.
And a report questioned whether Governor Whitmer advanced a big project in Saline Township before all local permits were in place.
That puts the governor's office on the defensive right after primary day. Washtenaw County residents could see major changes in power and water if it proceeds.
Quite a week of pushback. Any meetings listeners can attend in the next day or two?
We don't have any major public meetings on the tracker for tomorrow or the immediate days ahead.
Fair enough. Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Monroe Township Seeks to Dismiss $300M Data Center Lawsuit
